entries.title: English at a glance
body: English is a Germanic language that took in a huge amount of French and Latin vocabulary, so it often has two words for one idea: ask and inquire, freedom and liberty.

It has very little inflection: nouns only change for plural and possession, and verbs have at most five forms (go, goes, went, gone, going). Word order, subject then verb then object, does most of the grammatical work, so it is strict.
Spelling preserves older pronunciations and many borrowings, so it is a poor guide to sound.

examples.t: The dog bit the man. · The man bit the dog.
examples.e: Swapping the order swaps who did what.

entries.title: Spelling and sound don't match
entries.body: The same letters can spell different sounds, and the same sound can be spelled many ways. Learn the pronunciation together with each new word, and use a dictionary's phonetic spelling when unsure.

entries.title: Stress and the schwa
body: English is stress-timed: stressed syllables are long and loud, and unstressed ones shrink, usually to the weak vowel schwa /ə/, the most common sound in English.
Stress can change the word class. Many two-syllable words are nouns with stress on the first syllable and verbs with stress on the second.

examples.e: the stress moves, and the other vowels become schwa

entries.title: Saying -ed and -s endings
entries.body: The past ending -ed and the plural or third-person -s each have three pronunciations, decided by the sound before them.

rows: voiceless sounds: p, k, s, sh, ch, f

entries.title: The two th sounds
entries.body: Put the tip of the tongue lightly between the teeth and blow. Voiceless /θ/ is just air; voiced /ð/ adds the voice. The voiced one is in the most common words: the, this, that, they, there, then.

entries.title: a, an and the
body: Use {a / an} for one countable thing that is new to the listener. Choose by sound, not letter: an before a vowel sound, a before a consonant sound.
Use {the} when the listener knows which one you mean: it was mentioned, it is unique, or the context makes it clear. Use no article for things in general in the plural or uncountable.

examples.e: the sound decides, not the letter

examples.t: I saw a cat. {The} cat was black.

examples.e: cats and milk in general: no article

entries.title: Countable and uncountable nouns
entries.body: Uncountable nouns have no plural and don't take a / an. Some that are countable in other languages are uncountable in English: advice, information, furniture, luggage, news, homework, bread. Count them with a piece of, a slice of, a bottle of.

examples.e: A finished time: present perfect is not possible with yesterday.

entries.title: Common irregular verbs
entries.body: Around 200 verbs are irregular, and they are the most frequent ones. Learn three forms of each: base, past and past participle.

entries.title: Questions and negatives with do
entries.body: Most verbs need the helper do (does, did) to make questions and negatives; the main verb goes back to its base form. Be, modal verbs (can, must, will…) and other helpers (have in perfect tenses) swap places with the subject instead.

examples.t: {Do} you like tea? · She {doesn't} work here.
examples.e: do and does carry the tense and the -s
the main verb is in the base form

examples.t: {Are} you ready? · {Can} you swim? · {Have} you eaten?
examples.e: be, modals and helpers just swap

entries.title: Modal verbs
entries.body: Modals never take -s, are followed by the base form without to, and form questions and negatives on their own.

head: Modal
Typical meaning
Example
rows: Can I sit here? I could swim when I was five.
It might rain. May I come in?
You must wear a seatbelt. She must be tired.
I'll help. Would you like tea?

entries.title: Phrasal verbs
entries.body: A verb plus a small word (up, out, off, on…) often has a meaning you can't guess from the parts. They are everywhere in speech, where a phrasal verb usually replaces a more formal Latin-based verb.

entries.title: Order of adjectives
entries.body: When several adjectives come before a noun, native speakers follow a fixed order without thinking about it: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose. In practice, more than two or three is rare.

examples.e: not: a leather black big sofa

entries.title: Polite requests
entries.body: English signals politeness with indirect forms rather than special pronouns. A bare imperative (Give me…) can sound rude even with please.

examples.t: Could you pass the salt, please?
Would you mind closing the window?
examples.e: more polite; answer No, not at all to agree

examples.t: I was wondering if you could help me.

examples.e: to get attention or get past someone
